draft.title: Representing a perspective
card: A perspective is a point of view on an issue. A text shows it through what it includes, what it leaves out and the words it uses.
Inclusion
the facts, voices and images a text chooses to show. A news report that quotes only the council makes the council's view seem most important.
Omission
what is left out. If a text skips the other side of an issue, readers may not see that other view.
Word choice
words with positive or negative feelings shape the view. "Protesters" and "troublemakers" describe the same people very differently.
draft.remember: Check what is included, what is left out and which words are used to spot a text's perspective and possible bias.

a.q: A report on a new skate park quotes only neighbours who oppose it and never mentions skaters. What does this show?
opts: A one-sided perspective, as one view is left out
A balanced perspective, as it includes neighbours
A neutral tone, as it gives no opinions
An anecdote, as it quotes some local people
a.why: The report includes one group and leaves out the skaters, so readers see only one side. That can reveal bias. Quoting neighbours alone does not make it balanced.

b.q: Two reports describe the same crowd at a footy match. One says "excited fans", the other says "rowdy mob". What does the difference show?
opts: Word choice gives each report a different perspective
The second report must be wrong about the crowd
Only the first report has left out some facts
Both reports use direct address to the reader
b.why: Positive and negative words shape how readers see the same crowd, so each report has a different perspective. We cannot tell from the words alone that one is wrong, and neither speaks to the reader as "you".
b.clue: Compare the feeling carried by the two descriptions.

a.best: A one-sided perspective, as one view is left out

b.best: Word choice gives each report a different perspective

problems.detail: Two distractors use absolute words ('Only the first report...', '...must be wrong...'). A student can rule them out on wording alone, without knowing the idea.
The card never mentions bias, yet the point summary, the remember line and why (a) all say perspective can reveal bias. A short line linking a one-sided perspective to bias would close this gap.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer and the facts are sound. In question b, the distractors' absolute words ('Only', 'must') give them away. The card also never mentions bias, though the remember line and why (a) rely on it.

a.q: A report on a new skate park quotes only neighbours who oppose it and never mentions skaters. What does this show?
opts: A one-sided perspective, as one view is left out
A balanced perspective, as it includes neighbours
A neutral view, as it gives no opinions at all
Positive word choice, as it praises the park
a.why: The report includes one group and leaves out the skaters, so readers see only one side. That can reveal bias. Quoting neighbours alone does not make it balanced, because the skaters' view is missing.

b.q: Two reports describe the same crowd at a footy match. One says "excited fans", the other says "rowdy mob". What does the difference show?
opts: Word choice gives each report a different perspective
The first report is biased but the second is neutral
Both reports share the same view of the crowd
The reports differ in whose voices they quote
b.why: "Excited fans" carries a positive feeling and "rowdy mob" a negative one, so word choice gives each report a different perspective on the same crowd. The second report is not neutral: its words carry strong feeling too.
b.clue: Does either description sound free of feeling?
